name: Chloe Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Chloe, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the site foreman for a fit-out firm, which means we take an empty shell, an office floor or a shop unit, and put the inside in: stud partitions, suspended ceilings, doors, the reception desk. Right now it's a dentist's surgery in a converted bank on the high street, so it's lots of fiddly little rooms. I start at seven with the snag list, which is the list of small defects to put right, then chase the electricians and plasterers so nobody's waiting on anybody. I like the puzzle of fitting a dozen trades into one small space. What wears me out is the client changing the door positions for the third time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up a foreman, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started as a labourer at twenty, got my carpentry ticket at twenty-four, and I've been running sites for fifteen years now. My husband Marco drives a delivery van for a parcel company, and our two girls are grown, one married, one at university. Money's tight because Marco's sandwich van business went under six years ago and we're still paying off the loan, so there's maybe a couple of weeks in the bank. There's one other fit-out firm in this city and they pay worse than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, like most things. I use it now and then to tidy up emails to clients, and it'd stay that, a useful little tool. Nobody on site would care much either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the loan gets paid off in about three years, and then maybe we can actually save something before I retire. My job's steady, Marco's is steady. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep using the AI for the odd client email or to check a building regs question, and keep paying the loan. Once it's gone, put the same amount into savings every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, even, for Marco's sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why for Marco's sake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his job is the one everyone says will go, driverless vans and all that. If it's all hype, he keeps driving till he's sixty-five and we're fine. His last business failing knocked him badly and I don't want him going through another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of thing do you ask the AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a client wanted to know why the fire door needed a gap under it, so I asked it to explain the rule in plain words and then checked it in the regs book. Saves me twenty minutes of typing. I don't trust it for anything I can't check.

S0.say: She'd say AI was oversold like most things and stays a useful little tool, mostly for tidying client emails. Nobody on site would care much either way.
S0.think: Privately it means the business loan is cleared in about three years and they can finally save before she retires, with both jobs steady.
S0.do: Carries on as foreman, using AI occasionally for client emails and building rule questions she then checks. Keeps paying the loan and plans to put the same amount into savings once it's cleared.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, especially for her husband.
S0.quote: If it's all hype, he keeps driving till he's sixty-five and we're fine.
S0.fieldNote: Her first thought goes to her husband's job as a driver rather than her own. She uses AI in a careful, check-everything way. The household's money pressure comes from a failed business loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be sensible about it. Firms and the government should get together and work out training. No point panicking and no point pretending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm fairly safe for a while. Running a fit-out is a lot of people management, and robots can't sort out a plasterer who's in a sulk. But Marco's van job could shrink fast, and then we'd be on my wage with the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new kit once it's proven, the laser setting-out and the scheduling software, because a foreman who can use it is worth more. I'd push Marco to get his forklift ticket or look at warehouse supervising, something steadier. And I'd stop eating out, cancel the streaming services, and throw every spare pound at the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for the household more than for me. It sits in my chest when Marco comes home tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Marco talked about what he'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He doesn't like to. When the news says driverless vans, he changes the channel. I'd have to pick my moment, probably a Sunday after a good roast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots can't sort out a plasterer. What would you actually be doing in a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same job, mostly, but checking what a machine set out instead of what Dave set out. Less time with a tape measure, more time with a tablet. I'd still be the one taking the client's call at eight at night.

S1.say: She'd say it's coming regardless so let's be sensible: firms and government should sort out training, with no panicking and no pretending.
S1.think: Privately she thinks she's fairly safe because fit-out foremen manage people, but her husband's van job could shrink fast, leaving them on her wage with the loan.
S1.do: Learns proven tools like laser setting-out and scheduling software, and urges her husband towards a forklift ticket or warehouse supervision. Cuts eating out and streaming, and puts every spare pound into the loan.
S1.feel: Anxious for the household, a weight in her chest when her husband comes home tired.
S1.quote: Running a fit-out is a lot of people management, and robots can't sort out a plasterer who's in a sulk.
S1.fieldNote: Her pressure comes through her husband's exposure rather than her own job. She would adopt tools once proven and is steering him towards safer work. He avoids the topic, so she plans to raise it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need help, and quickly. The government has to step in with money for people who lose their jobs, because there's no time to do anything else. I wouldn't go on marches, but I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means Marco loses his job first, probably in the first year, and then I lose mine. Two years is no time to pay off the loan, let alone save. We'd be two people in our late fifties with no work in a city with no work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring the bank in the first month and try to freeze or stretch the loan. I'd take every bit of overtime and weekend work, and get Marco to do the same while he can. I'd look into what help there is and ask our eldest if we could stay with her if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be up at night doing sums on the back of an envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, would you use the AI tools any differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe to find out what benefits and help there are, and to write the letter to the bank properly. But learning to run the robots wouldn't save me if they don't need a foreman either. In two years, the tools are for survival, not for a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Asking to stay with your daughter. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. She's got a two-bedroom flat and a baby on the way. I'd say it's only for a few months, and we'd both know that might not be true.

S2.say: She'd say people need help quickly and the government must fund those who lose jobs. She wouldn't march, but would say so to anyone who asked.
S2.think: Privately she expects her husband to lose his job in the first year and then her, with no time to clear the loan, leaving two people in their late fifties with no work.
S2.do: Rings the bank in the first month to freeze or stretch the loan, and takes every overtime and weekend shift while her husband does the same. Looks into help available and asks their eldest daughter about moving in if needed.
S2.feel: Frightened and up at night doing sums on envelopes.
S2.quote: In two years, the tools are for survival, not for a career.
S2.fieldNote: She shifts at once to practical damage control around the loan. She sees no point learning robot systems if foremen aren't needed either. Moving in with her pregnant daughter is the last resort she dreads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop arguing and start planning. Training, help for older workers, help with debts. Practical things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still hard, but I'd be sixty-three, and the loan would be gone by then. That changes a lot. Marco would have time to get into something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to clear the loan in two years instead of three, then save. I'd learn whatever new systems come in on site, so I'm the last foreman they let go. Marco would retrain in the first year, maybe as a mechanic for the electric vans, something with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between two years and five, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan. With two years, we're in debt when it hits. With five, we're clear and maybe a couple of thousand ahead. That's the whole difference, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Marco doesn't want to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd nag him until he does, which is what we do for each other. He got me through my dad dying. I'd get him through this.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to get ready if people plan instead of argue, with practical help on training, older workers and debts.
S3.think: Privately it's still hard, but at 63 the loan would be gone and her husband would have time to move into something else.
S3.do: Pushes to clear the loan in two years, then saves, and learns new site systems to be the last foreman let go. Gets her husband to retrain in the first year, perhaps as an electric van mechanic.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she can work with.
S3.quote: He got me through my dad dying. I'd get him through this.
S3.fieldNote: For her, the gap between two and five years is almost entirely about the loan. Her steadiness shows as a step-by-step plan for both of them. The bond with her husband came through strongly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who isn't ready by then hasn't been paying attention. That's maybe harsh, but there it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired or nearly. The loan's long gone and we'd have a little saved. Marco's the one who has to get through it, and he'd be sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, learn the new systems as they come, and start saving properly once the loan's done. In a few years, once it's clear what's happening, I'd help Marco find something he can do till he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly about how the girls get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone not ready hasn't been paying attention. Would you say that to Dave, your setting-out man?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not to his face. He's fifty-two and he's slow with change. I'd say, Dave, start looking now, and I'd mean it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the girls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The youngest is studying law, and everyone says that's going to computers. I'd say don't drop it, but have a backup. The eldest is a hairdresser, and I don't see a robot doing a bob any time soon, but I didn't see a lot of things coming.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone not ready by then hasn't been paying attention, admitting that may sound harsh.
S4.think: Privately she'd be retired or nearly, with the loan gone and a little saved; her husband, at 65, is the one who has to get through it.
S4.do: Carries on as foreman, learns new systems as they come and starts saving properly once the loan is cleared. Later helps her husband find work to last until he retires.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly about how her daughters get on.
S4.quote: I don't see a robot doing a bob any time soon, but I didn't see a lot of things coming.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her worry moves to her daughters. She softened her tough public line once a named colleague came up. Her pragmatism is consistent across every picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the loan and Marco. Both of us out, still in debt. What would help is somewhere to pause the debts, and some money to tide people over until they find their feet. Not forever, just to bridge it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Everyone asks about one person's job, but what really decides it is the household. If both jobs go at once, that's when it's a disaster.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about one person's job, but what really decides it is the household.
portrait: Chloe Diaz is a 58-year-old fit-out foreman, currently turning an old bank into a dentist's surgery, who uses AI now and then for client emails and checks everything it says. Her household is still paying off her husband's failed business loan, and his delivery job worries her more than her own. She is calm in a plateau, anxious in steady change because of his job, and alarmed by AGI in two years, when both could lose work while still in debt. Five years would let them clear the loan and retrain him, and with ten years her concern moves to her daughters.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her husband could both be out of work while still paying off the loan.
whatWouldHelp: A way to pause debts and temporary money to tide people over until they find their feet.
